why: Cortisol is highest in the first hour after waking and lowest around midnight to early sleep.
source: Weitzman et al. 1971 J Clin Endocrinol Metab; Debono et al. 2009 J Clin Endocrinol Metab

why: The cortisol awakening response peaks about 30-45 minutes after waking, so with a 07:00 wake-up the day's top value falls around 07:30-08:00.
source: Pruessner et al. 1997 Life Sci; Stalder et al. 2016 Psychoneuroendocrinology (CAR expert consensus)

why: ACTH rises in the second half of the night and leads cortisol by a short time, with a late-evening low and a smaller day-night swing than cortisol.
source: Krieger et al. 1971 J Clin Endocrinol Metab; Horrocks et al. 1990 Clin Endocrinol

why: Melatonin starts rising about 2 h before habitual sleep (dim-light onset near 21:00), peaks around 02:00-04:00 and is near zero during daylight hours.
source: Arendt 2005 J Biol Rhythms; Burgess & Fogg 2008 PLoS One; Lewy et al. 1999

why: Basal-forebrain adenosine builds up across waking and is cleared during sleep, so it is highest near bedtime and lowest on waking.
source: Porkka-Heiskanen et al. 1997 Science; Porkka-Heiskanen & Kalinchuk 2011 Sleep Med Rev (largely animal data)

why: Felt sleepiness is high around bedtime and in the early-morning circadian low, and low through the waking day.
source: Borbely 1982 Hum Neurobiol (two-process model); Akerstedt & Gillberg 1990 Int J Neurosci (KSS)

why: Daytime sleepiness is lowest in late morning; a modest post-lunch dip around 13:00-16:00 makes early afternoon sleepier, but the dip is small and varies a lot between people.
source: Monk 2005 Clin Sports Med (post-lunch dip); Carrier & Monk 2000 Chronobiol Int

why: Subjective alertness is high from late morning to early evening and lowest around 03:00-06:00 at the circadian low.
source: Folkard & Akerstedt 1987; Dijk et al. 1992 J Sleep Res

why: Attention and working-memory performance roughly track body temperature and alertness, best in the late morning to early evening and worst near 04:00-06:00.
source: Schmidt et al. 2007 Cogn Neuropsychol; Blatter & Cajochen 2007 Physiol Behav

why: Ghrelin rises before each meal (here 07:30, 12:30, 19:00) and drops after eating; its highest levels are before dinner and during the night, and its lowest are after breakfast.
source: Cummings et al. 2001 Diabetes; Cummings et al. 2004 Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab

why: Hunger peaks just before meals, with the biggest peak before the 19:00 dinner because of the long gap after lunch and the evening high point of circadian appetite; it is lowest after breakfast.
source: Scheer et al. 2013 Obesity (circadian appetite peak ~20:00, trough ~08:00); Cummings et al. 2004

why: Many people with major depression, especially the melancholic type, feel worst in the morning and better by evening, but this pattern is absent or reversed in a large minority.
source: Wirz-Justice 2008 Int Clin Psychopharmacol; Rusting & Larsen 1998

why: Depression usually keeps the morning cortisol peak but raises evening levels, giving a flatter day-night slope.
source: Deuschle et al. 1997 J Clin Endocrinol Metab; Stetler & Miller 2011 Psychosom Med (meta-analysis)

why: Nightly melatonin in depression is often reported as somewhat lower or shifted in timing, but findings disagree across studies.
source: Srinivasan et al. 2006 Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat (review); Hasler et al. 2010 Psychiatry Res

why: Chronic stress is linked to a flatter diurnal cortisol slope, with lower morning and higher evening levels than usual.
source: Adam et al. 2017 Psychoneuroendocrinology (meta-analysis); Miller, Chen & Zhou 2007 Psychol Bull

why: With waking at 06:00 the awakening peak comes earlier, and chronic short sleep raises evening cortisol, making the slope somewhat flatter.
source: Spiegel, Leproult & Van Cauter 1999 Lancet; Leproult et al. 1997 Sleep

why: Melatonin timing is set mainly by the body clock, so the night peak stays near 02:00-04:00, though light exposure while awake until 01:00 can suppress or slightly delay it.
source: Zeitzer et al. 2000 J Physiol (light suppression); Burgess & Eastman 2006 J Physiol

why: Short sleepers are sleepiest from late evening to early morning, and their daytime sleepiness is higher than typical at all hours.
source: Van Dongen et al. 2003 Sleep; Belenky et al. 2003 J Sleep Res

why: Adenosine keeps building until the late 01:00 bedtime and is lowest just after the short sleep ends.
source: Porkka-Heiskanen et al. 1997 Science; Elmenhorst et al. 2007 J Neurosci (A1 receptor PET after sleep loss)

why: Problems keeping attention and poorer working memory are core features of ADHD and show up consistently on tests.
source: Willcutt et al. 2005 Biol Psychiatry (meta-analysis); Huang-Pollock et al. 2012 J Abnorm Psychol

why: People with ADHD are more easily distracted by noise and activity around them, so a busy place makes the gap in attention at least as large.
source: Gumenyuk et al. 2005 Neurosci Lett; Pelletier et al. 2016 J Atten Disord

why: Reduced drive for delayed or dull rewards is reported in ADHD, but the reward-deficit and dopamine-deficit accounts are contested and motivation for interesting tasks can be normal or high.
source: Sonuga-Barke 2003 Neurosci Biobehav Rev; Volkow et al. 2009 JAMA; Plichta & Scheres 2014 Neurosci Biobehav Rev

why: Anxiety is common alongside ADHD (roughly a quarter to half of adults), but it is not a core feature.
source: Kessler et al. 2006 Am J Psychiatry; Reimherr et al. 2017 Psychiatry Res

why: Many people with ADHD have a body clock about an hour later than usual, so they feel less sleepy at the normal bedtime.
source: Van Veen et al. 2010 Biol Psychiatry; Coogan & McGowan 2017 Atten Defic Hyperact Disord (review)

why: ADHD does not change resting breathing drive.
source: No known respiratory phenotype in ADHD; DSM-5 criteria; standard clinical physiology

why: Most autistic people report sensory over-responsiveness, and loud, bright, crowded places often cause distress and anxiety.
source: Green & Ben-Sasson 2010 J Autism Dev Disord; Ben-Sasson et al. 2009 J Autism Dev Disord (meta-analysis)

why: Sensory overload in noisy, busy settings makes it harder for many autistic people to focus.
source: Remington & Fairnie 2017 Cognition; Robertson & Simmons 2013 J Autism Dev Disord

why: Distress from sensory overload lowers mood in crowded, loud places.
source: MacLennan et al. 2021 Autism (sensory overload qualitative/quant review); Ben-Sasson et al. 2009

why: About 40% of autistic people have an anxiety disorder, so baseline anxiety is somewhat higher even in a calm setting.
source: van Steensel et al. 2011 Clin Child Fam Psychol Rev; Hollocks et al. 2019 Psychol Med (meta-analyses)

why: Physiological over-arousal in busy sensory settings is reported, but evidence is mixed and the excitation/inhibition model behind it is contested.
source: Rubenstein & Merzenich 2003 Genes Brain Behav (E/I model); Lydon et al. 2016 J Autism Dev Disord (arousal review, mixed); Dickinson et al. 2016

why: Autistic sensory sensitivity is not the altered, psychedelic-like perception this scale measures, and in a quiet room there is nothing to be overwhelmed by.
source: DSM-5 sensory criteria; Robertson & Baron-Cohen 2017 Nat Rev Neurosci

why: Autism does not change resting breathing drive.
source: No known respiratory phenotype in idiopathic autism; standard clinical physiology

why: Persistent low mood is the defining symptom of major depression.
source: DSM-5; Hamilton 1960 / MADRS norms

why: Loss of interest and drive (anhedonia, low effort for rewards) is a core feature of depression.
source: Treadway & Zald 2011 Neurosci Biobehav Rev; Pizzagalli 2014 Annu Rev Clin Psychol

why: Depression brings moderate problems with attention and working memory.
source: Rock et al. 2014 Psychol Med (meta-analysis); Snyder 2013 Psychol Bull

why: Anxiety symptoms accompany most episodes of major depression.
source: Kessler et al. 2003 JAMA; Fava et al. 2008 Am J Psychiatry (anxious depression)

why: Fatigue and daytime tiredness are common in depression, but insomnia and hypersomnia both occur, so daytime sleepiness varies.
source: Tylee et al. 1999 Int Clin Psychopharmacol (DEPRES); Ferentinos et al. 2009

why: Appetite loss is somewhat more common than appetite gain in depression, but many people (atypical type) eat more, so the average direction is uncertain.
source: Simmons et al. 2016 JAMA Psychiatry; Kendler et al. DSM appetite symptom data

why: Depression does not change resting breathing drive.
source: Standard clinical physiology; no respiratory phenotype in MDD

why: People with depression start with lower mood and recover less from a stressor, so their mood stays clearly below typical during stress.
source: Bylsma et al. 2008 Clin Psychol Rev; Peeters et al. 2003 J Abnorm Psychol

why: Constant, hard-to-control worry and tension, even in calm settings, is the defining feature of generalised anxiety disorder.
source: DSM-5; Newman et al. 2013 Annu Rev Clin Psychol

why: People with GAD report more anxiety during a stressor, although their bodily stress response is sometimes the same or even blunted.
source: Hoehn-Saric et al. 1989 Arch Gen Psychiatry; Newman & Llera 2011 Clin Psychol Rev

why: Worry takes up working memory and pulls attention away from the task at hand.
source: Eysenck et al. 2007 Emotion (attentional control theory); Moran 2016 Psychol Bull (meta-analysis)

why: In GAD (unlike panic disorder), resting breathing drive is essentially normal.
source: Wilhelm et al. 2001 Biol Psychiatry; Grassi et al. 2014 (respiratory findings mainly in panic disorder)

why: Long-term stress raises everyday tension and anxiety.
source: McEwen 2008 Eur J Pharmacol; Cohen et al. 1983 Perceived Stress Scale correlates

why: Chronic stress lowers mood and is a major risk factor for depression.
source: Hammen 2005 Annu Rev Clin Psychol; Kendler et al. 1999 Am J Psychiatry

why: Chronic stress impairs prefrontal attention control and flexibility, which recover once the stress ends.
source: Liston et al. 2009 PNAS; Arnsten 2009 Nat Rev Neurosci

why: People under ongoing stress often feel a new stressor more strongly, but studies of the acute response show both sensitised and blunted patterns.
source: Miller, Chen & Zhou 2007 Psychol Bull; McEwen 1998 NEJM (allostatic load)

why: Sleeping 5 hours a night builds steady sleep debt that makes people clearly sleepier during the day.
source: Van Dongen et al. 2003 Sleep; Belenky et al. 2003 J Sleep Res

why: Repeated short sleep steadily worsens sustained attention, and people underestimate how impaired they are.
source: Van Dongen et al. 2003 Sleep; Lim & Dinges 2010 Psychol Bull (meta-analysis)

why: A week of about 5 h sleep a night lowers mood and raises irritability.
source: Dinges et al. 1997 Sleep; Short et al. 2020 / Tomaso et al. 2021 Psychol Bull (meta-analysis)

why: Sleep loss raises anxiety and strengthens the brain's threat response.
source: Ben Simon et al. 2020 Nat Hum Behav; Pires et al. 2016 Neurosci Biobehav Rev (meta-analysis)

why: After short sleep, people report more anxiety and more stress in response to a mild stressor.
source: Minkel et al. 2012 Emotion; Goldstein et al. 2013 J Neurosci

why: Short sleep raises ghrelin, lowers leptin and increases hunger and calorie intake.
source: Spiegel et al. 2004 Ann Intern Med; Al Khatib et al. 2017 Eur J Clin Nutr (meta-analysis)

why: Short sleep can slightly blunt the breathing response to high CO2, but resting breathing drive while awake is essentially unchanged.
source: White et al. 1983 Am Rev Respir Dis; Spengler & Shea 2000 Am J Respir Crit Care Med
